sections.title: The Core Operating System: The Kernel
Single Directory Hierarchy, Directories, Links, and Files
Process Groups and Shell Job Control
Sessions, Controlling Terminals, and Controlling Processes

questions.prompt: Linux is a _preemptive_ multitasking OS. What does "preemptive" mean?
options: Processes give up the CPU voluntarily when finished
The kernel's scheduler decides which process gets the CPU and for how long
Many processes can be in memory at the same time
Processes run in kernel mode by default
questions.answer: The kernel's scheduler decides which process gets the CPU and for how long
questions.hint: Multitasking and preemptive are two separate ideas.
questions.explanation: Multitasking means many processes share memory and the CPU. Preemptive means the kernel scheduler, not the processes, controls CPU allocation.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of virtual memory management named in the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Processes are isolated from each other and from the kernel
Only part of a process needs to be in RAM, so more processes fit
Programs no longer need system calls to read files
The kernel no longer needs a scheduler
answers: Processes are isolated from each other and from the kernel
Only part of a process needs to be in RAM, so more processes fit
questions.explanation: Isolation, and keeping only part of each process in RAM. The second leads to better CPU utilization because there's more likely to be a runnable process.

questions.prompt: A CPU in user mode tries to access memory marked as kernel space. What happens?
options: The access succeeds but is logged
The CPU switches to kernel mode automatically
questions.explanation: In user mode only user-space memory is accessible. Touching kernel space raises a hardware exception, which is how the kernel is protected.

questions.prompt: Which operations can only be performed in kernel mode, according to the chapter?
options: Calling a function in a shared library
questions.explanation: Halting, memory-management hardware and starting device I/O are privileged. Calling library code is ordinary user-mode execution.

questions.prompt: A process can create a new process by itself, without the kernel's involvement.
questions.explanation: A process can only _request_ that the kernel create a process. "A process creates a process" is shorthand for that request.

questions.prompt: What is the usual pathname of the Linux kernel executable?
questions.explanation: `/boot/vmlinuz`. The _z_ replaces the final _x_ of vmunix/vmlinux to show that it's a compressed executable.

questions.prompt: Match each shell to what it's known for.

pairs.definition: The original; standard on Seventh Edition UNIX and present on every UNIX
C-like syntax, added history and aliases, not Bourne compatible
Bourne compatible with csh-style interactive features, basis of POSIX.2
GNU's reimplementation of the Bourne shell, most common on Linux

questions.explanation: Bourne came first. Bill Joy's C shell added interactive features but broke compatibility. Korn combined the two. Bash is GNU's reimplementation.

questions.prompt: On UNIX systems, the shell is part of the kernel.
questions.explanation: On UNIX the shell is an ordinary user process, so different users can run different shells at once.

questions.prompt: What user ID does the superuser have?
questions.explanation: UID 0, normally with the login name `root`. It bypasses all permission checks.

questions.prompt: For security, where is the encrypted password usually stored instead of `/etc/passwd`?
questions.explanation: The shadow password file is readable only by privileged users, unlike `/etc/passwd`.

questions.prompt: Besides the login name and UID, which fields does a user's `/etc/passwd` line contain?
options: Group ID of the user's first group
List of all groups the user belongs to
answers: Group ID of the user's first group
questions.explanation: Group membership lists are in `/etc/group`. The passwd line has only the first group's GID.

questions.prompt: What is a symbolic link?
options: A second directory entry pointing directly to the same file
A specially marked file whose contents are the name of another file
A copy of a file that updates automatically
The `.` and `..` entries of a directory
questions.answer: A specially marked file whose contents are the name of another file
questions.explanation: A hard link is a filename-plus-pointer entry in a directory. A symlink is a file containing a pathname, its target.

questions.prompt: What is a symbolic link called when its target doesn't exist?
questions.explanation: A dangling link.

questions.prompt: In this shell session, what does the last command print?
questions.explanation: In the root directory, `..` is a link to root itself, so `/..` is `/`.

questions.prompt: Which filename is safest under the SUSv3 portable filename character set?
questions.explanation: The portable set is `[-._a-zA-Z0-9]`. Spaces and parentheses need escaping, and a leading hyphen looks like an option.

questions.prompt: You want to delete a file you don't own from a shared directory. Which permission matters?
questions.hint: Deleting removes a filename from a table. What holds that table?
questions.explanation: Directory write permission allows adding, removing and renaming entries. Deleting changes the directory, not the file.

questions.prompt: Match each permission bit **on a directory** to what it allows.
questions.explanation: On directories, execute is also called _search_ permission.

questions.prompt: From the directory `/home/avr`, which relative pathname reaches `/home/mtk/.bashrc`?
questions.explanation: `..` goes up to `/home`, then down into `mtk`. A leading `/` would make it absolute.

questions.prompt: How does a UNIX program detect end-of-file?
options: The file ends with a null byte
questions.explanation: EOF is a read that returns no data. -1 indicates an error.

questions.prompt: Match each file descriptor to its stream.
questions.explanation: A process started by the shell normally inherits all three, connected to the terminal.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the idea that the same system calls (`open`, `read`, `write`, `close`) work on all file types, including devices?
questions.explanation: Universality of I/O. The kernel translates the calls into file-system or device-driver operations.

questions.prompt: A program is run as `./greet hello world`. What is `argc`?
questions.explanation: `argv[0]` is the program name, so `./greet`, `hello`, `world` makes 3.

questions.prompt: Which of these are examples of filters given in the chapter?
questions.explanation: A filter reads stdin, transforms the data, and writes stdout. `ls` lists a directory rather than transforming input.

questions.prompt: Order the process memory segments from **lowest** to **highest** address, as in the note's layout diagram.
questions.explanation: Text (instructions) is lowest, then Data (static variables), then Heap (grows up), with the Stack at the top (grows down).

questions.prompt: After `fork()`, which part of the parent's memory does the child **share** rather than copy?
questions.explanation: Data, stack and heap are copied. The read-only program text is shared.

questions.prompt: There is a C library function named `exec()`.
questions.explanation: "exec()" is shorthand for the family (`execve`, `execl`, `execvp`, …). No function is named `exec()` itself.

questions.prompt: Which IDs does the kernel use to decide whether a process may open a protected file?
options: Effective UID, effective GID and supplementary GIDs
questions.answer: Effective UID, effective GID and supplementary GIDs
questions.explanation: Real IDs say who owns the process. Permission checks use the effective IDs plus supplementary groups.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `false` exits with a nonzero status (1), and `$?` holds the last command's termination status.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `init` is true?
options: It has PID 1 and every other process descends from it
questions.answer: It has PID 1 and every other process descends from it
questions.explanation: The kernel creates init at boot from `/sbin/init`. It's PID 1, runs as superuser, can't be killed, and ends only at shutdown.

questions.prompt: An unprivileged process has an open-files soft limit of 1024 and hard limit of 4096. What can it do?
options: Raise the soft limit to 4096, or lower the hard limit
Nothing; only root can change limits
questions.answer: Raise the soft limit to 4096, or lower the hard limit
questions.explanation: Unprivileged: soft can go anywhere from 0 to hard, and hard can only be lowered.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics define a daemon?
options: Long-lived, often from boot to shutdown
Runs in the background with no controlling terminal
answers: Long-lived, often from boot to shutdown
Runs in the background with no controlling terminal
questions.explanation: Long-lived and backgrounded with no controlling terminal. Examples are `syslogd` and `httpd`.

questions.prompt: In a **private** file mapping, what happens to your changes?
options: They're written to the file and visible to other processes
They're written to the file but not visible to others
They're neither visible to other processes nor written to the file
The mapping is read-only, so changes aren't allowed
questions.answer: They're neither visible to other processes nor written to the file
questions.explanation: Shared mappings propagate changes to other processes and the file. Private mappings do neither.

questions.prompt: What are the pages of an anonymous mapping initialized to?
questions.explanation: Anonymous mappings have no backing file, so pages start zero-filled.

questions.prompt: A bug is fixed in a function that many programs use. With which library type do those programs get the fix without being relinked?
questions.explanation: Statically linked programs contain their own copy and must be relinked. Shared libraries are loaded at run time by the dynamic linker.

questions.prompt: Match each IPC mechanism to its main use.

pairs.definition: Let processes see each other's changes immediately

questions.explanation: See the IPC table in §2.10 of the note.

questions.prompt: FIFOs and UNIX domain sockets do much the same job. Why do both exist?
options: One is for threads, the other for processes
FIFOs came from System V and sockets from BSD
POSIX requires two mechanisms for redundancy
questions.answer: FIFOs came from System V and sockets from BSD
questions.explanation: Overlapping IPC mechanisms are a result of different UNIX lineages and standards.

questions.prompt: A signal is generated while it's in the process's signal mask. What happens?
options: It stays pending until it's unblocked
questions.answer: It stays pending until it's unblocked
questions.explanation: Blocked signals remain pending and are delivered once removed from the mask.

questions.prompt: Which events does the chapter list as causing the kernel to send a signal?
options: A timer set by the process expires
The process accesses an invalid memory address
answers: A timer set by the process expires
The process accesses an invalid memory address
questions.explanation: The first four are the chapter's examples. Opening a file doesn't generate a signal.

questions.prompt: What does each thread have its own copy of?
questions.explanation: Threads share code, data and heap, but each has its own stack for local variables and call linkage.

questions.prompt: You run `ls -l | sort -k5n | less` in bash. How are those processes organized?
options: Three processes in one process group, inside the shell's session
Three processes, each in its own session
Three processes in three process groups
questions.answer: Three processes in one process group, inside the shell's session
questions.explanation: One process per command, and a job-control shell puts the whole pipeline in one process group (a job) within its session. That's how Ctrl-Z stops the whole pipeline.

questions.prompt: Order from **largest** to **smallest** container.
questions.explanation: A session holds process groups, a process group holds processes, and a process holds threads.

questions.prompt: You close a terminal window. Which process receives `SIGHUP`?
options: Every process in the background jobs
questions.explanation: The session leader became the controlling process when it opened the controlling terminal, and it gets SIGHUP on disconnect.

questions.prompt: A terminal can be the controlling terminal of several sessions at once.
questions.explanation: A terminal can be the controlling terminal of at most one session.

questions.prompt: Which are typical uses of pseudoterminals?
options: Terminal windows in a graphical desktop
answers: Terminal windows in a graphical desktop
questions.explanation: A pseudoterminal lets a driver program act as the user for a terminal-oriented program on the slave side.

questions.prompt: Calendar time counts seconds since midnight on which date (UTC)?
questions.explanation: 1 January 1970 UTC, the Epoch, close to the birth of UNIX.

questions.prompt: Time spent executing system calls on behalf of a process is counted as…
questions.explanation: System CPU time is time in kernel mode. User CPU time is time running your own code in user mode.

questions.prompt: What is the defining feature of a realtime application?
options: It runs faster than normal applications
Its response is guaranteed within a deadline after the triggering event
questions.answer: Its response is guaranteed within a deadline after the triggering event
questions.explanation: Many realtime systems are fast, but the defining factor is the guaranteed deadline.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `/proc` are true?
options: It's a virtual file system exposing kernel data structures
Any user can modify any file in it
answers: It's a virtual file system exposing kernel data structures
questions.explanation: Modifying files in `/proc` usually requires privilege.

questions.prompt: Which is **not** one of the chapter's reasons to put a service in a server?
questions.explanation: Clients and servers communicate _using_ IPC, so a server doesn't avoid it.

questions.prompt: `/usr/bin/passwd` is owned by root and has the set-user-ID bit. When a normal user runs it, what changes?
options: Both real and effective UID become 0
Nothing; the `s` bit only affects directories
questions.explanation: Set-user-ID gives the process an effective UID equal to the file owner's UID, here root. The real UID stays the user's own.
